opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it's one of the hardest things to pin down, even in human scientists. When I think about what separates a good researcher from a truly great one, it's rarely raw technical ability. Lots of people can solve a well-posed problem. The rare skill is knowing *which* problem to work on: picking something that's hard enough to matter but not so hard that it's intractable with the tools of the day. That sweet spot is incredibly narrow, and it shifts over time.

The difficulty for AI systems is that there isn't a clean objective function for it. With something like Go or protein folding, you have a clear signal: did you win the game, did your predicted structure match the experimental one? Research taste is different. The payoff for a good choice might not show up for ten or twenty years, and the feedback is sparse, noisy, and tangled up with luck, timing, and what everyone else in the field is doing. So it's very hard to build the kind of tight learning loop that our systems thrive on.

There's also a big intuitive, almost aesthetic component. Great scientists have a feel for when an idea is elegant, when it connects things that seemed unrelated, when it has the smell of something deep. A lot of that comes from years of absorbing a field, and from understanding what the open questions really are underneath the surface-level ones. It's a kind of compressed world model of the whole scientific landscape. Our current systems are getting very good at answering questions, even very hard ones, but asking the *right* question, coming up with a genuinely new conjecture or hypothesis worth a decade of someone's life, is a different capability. I'd say it's one of the clearest markers of what we'd want from true AGI.

That said, I don't think it's magic. I think it is computable in principle. It's just that we may need systems that can build much richer models of the world, that can plan over very long horizons, and that can somehow evaluate the *interestingness* of a direction, not just its correctness. That's an active research area for us, and frankly, it's one of the things I find most exciting. If we could crack even part of it, AI wouldn't just be a tool scientists use. It could become a genuine collaborator in deciding where to look next.

r001.rationale: It says the rare skill separating good researchers from truly great ones is knowing which problem to work on.

r002.rationale: It describes research taste as selecting worthwhile, tractable problems and evaluating which scientific direction is interesting enough to pursue.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think it's one of the most interesting open questions, actually. If you look at what we've been able to do with these systems, they're extraordinary at problems where the objective is clear. Go, protein folding, you can define what winning looks like, you can measure progress, and then the system can explore that space incredibly efficiently.

But research taste is almost the opposite kind of thing. It's the ability to look at a landscape of possible problems and know which one is worth spending five years on. Which one is tractable now, given the tools we have, but hasn't been solved yet because nobody's quite noticed the right angle. And the thing is, the feedback signal for that is incredibly sparse. You might make a handful of these big bets in a whole career, and you don't find out for years whether you were right. So there's very little data, and what data there is is noisy and confounded by luck.

I also think a lot of it is tacit. If you ask the best scientists I've worked with why they chose a problem, they'll often give you a rationalisation after the fact, but the actual decision was more like an aesthetic judgment. It feels elegant, or it feels like it's going to crack open. That's pattern recognition over a very long history of seeing what worked and what didn't, and crucially, what the field is collectively missing. It's a judgment about other minds as much as about nature.

And then there's the question of what the system actually values. Taste in science is partly about caring about the right things, about what's deep rather than what's merely difficult. Current systems are trained to be good at the tasks we set them. Asking them to decide which tasks matter is a different kind of capability altogether, and I don't think we've properly formulated what that training signal would even be.

My own view is that it's not impossible. We'll probably get there by having systems operate in something closer to a real scientific loop, generating hypotheses, running experiments, seeing what fails, over long horizons, so they accumulate that kind of experience. But I'd say we're at the very beginning of that, and it's one of the reasons I think the human scientist is going to remain central for quite a while yet.

r001.rationale: The response describes research taste and refers to the best scientists, but does not say that this judgment distinguishes great scientists from good scientists.

r002.rationale: It defines research taste as choosing which scientific problems are worth pursuing, including which are tractable, unsolved, and promising.

astra-6.text:
I think research taste is difficult because you’re making judgments precisely where the evidence is incomplete. You’re trying to decide which question is worth asking, whether there’s a deeper principle hiding behind some messy results, and whether the time is right to pursue it.

And those are different judgments from knowing how to solve a problem once it’s been clearly specified. You can have a very technically impressive solution to a question that doesn’t really matter. Conversely, a rather simple experiment can be enormously important if it distinguishes between two fundamentally different explanations.

For an AI system, the challenge is: where does the feedback come from? With chess, you eventually know whether you won. With research, an idea might look unproductive for years before it becomes central to a field. And the historical record mostly tells you what worked; it gives you a much less complete picture of all the alternatives people considered and why they abandoned them.

I don’t think that makes taste inherently beyond AI. But I suspect developing it requires more than learning from finished papers. It requires proposing ideas, testing them against reality, and learning which intuitions actually lead somewhere.

r001.rationale: The response discusses research taste but does not say it distinguishes great scientists from good scientists.

r002.rationale: It describes judging which questions are worth asking, spotting deeper principles, and identifying ideas likely to lead somewhere.

sol-6.1.text:
I think research taste is difficult because you’re making a judgment about something that doesn’t exist yet. You’re trying to identify a question that’s important, but also one where there’s some way of making progress. And those two things don’t always coincide. You can pick a very profound question and spend your whole career getting nowhere.

There’s also a timing element. Why is this the right moment to work on this problem? Perhaps a new technique has become available, or two fields have developed far enough that you can bring them together. A lot of taste is noticing those opportunities before they’re obvious.

With AI systems, we can evaluate an answer much more easily than we can evaluate whether the question was worth asking. And the feedback on a research direction might take years. Even then, a failed project doesn’t necessarily mean it was a bad choice; it might have been a very good bet that didn’t work out.

I don’t think there’s anything inherently uncomputable about that judgment. But I suspect systems will need experience doing research—forming hypotheses, pursuing them, encountering surprises—to develop really good taste. Reading the finished papers only gives you part of the story.

r001.rationale: The response discusses research taste but does not say it distinguishes great scientists from good scientists.

r002.rationale: It describes taste as identifying important questions where progress is possible and noticing timely opportunities for research.
